chunks: "At a high level, chips are made by building the transistors and wires on a silicon wafer, layer by layer, using a repeated cycle of deposit, pattern and etch.
You start from a very pure single-crystal silicon wafer, grown from sand that's been purified.

Then in the front end you build transistors: you grow or deposit thin films like silicon dioxide and the gate material, you use photolithography to define patterns in a light-sensitive resist, you etch away material or implant dopants through the openings to make the source, drain and wells, and you polish the surface flat.
That pattern, expose, etch loop is repeated for every layer, around fifty to a hundred times for a modern processor.
Once the transistors exist, the back end builds the wiring: several to more than a dozen layers of copper interconnect separated by insulators, with vias between them.
When the wafer is done, you probe-test every die, cut the wafer into individual dies, put the good ones in a package with bond wires or bumps, and test again.
The whole thing takes weeks to months in a cleanroom, and the key challenges are tiny feature sizes and yield: one particle or defect can ruin a die, so process control matters enormously."
